concept_00a4be873ec9_RhetoricalRole.OBJE.name: Machine Learning Objective_RhetoricalRole.OBJECTIVE
concept_00a4be873ec9_RhetoricalRole.OBJE.content: The objective of ML is to build a good predictive model.

concept_6394f58d859e_RhetoricalRole.DEFI.name: Good Predictive Model_RhetoricalRole.DEFINITION
concept_6394f58d859e_RhetoricalRole.DEFI.content: By “good”, we mean that the model should predict well to new data.

Q331309.name: overfitting
Q331309.content: production of an analysis that corresponds too closely or exactly to a particular set of data, and may therefore fail to fit additional data or predict future observations reliably

Q331309_RhetoricalRole.PROBLEM.name: overfitting_RhetoricalRole.PROBLEM
Q331309_RhetoricalRole.PROBLEM.content: A more complex and flexible model has a higher risk of overfitting.

Q17003119.name: bias–variance tradeoff
Q17003119.content: property of a set of predictive models whereby models with a lower bias in parameter estimation have a higher variance of the parameter estimates across samples, and vice versa

Q17003119_RhetoricalRole.DEFINITION.name: bias–variance tradeoff_RhetoricalRole.DEFINITION
Q17003119_RhetoricalRole.DEFINITION.content: The trade-off between complexity and flexibility can be depicted by the bias-variance tradeoff (Box 3).

concept_9ae3c1dd6809.name: General Ideal of Machine Learning Algorithms

concept_9ae3c1dd6809_RhetoricalRole.STAT.name: General Ideal of Machine Learning Algorithms_RhetoricalRole.STATEMENT
concept_9ae3c1dd6809_RhetoricalRole.STAT.content: The general ideal of Machine Learning algorithms is thus to take a certain algorithmic structure and then adjust their parameters to the data (training), while simultaneously adapt its complexity by optimizing the bias-variance trade-off so that the fitted model generalizes well to new data.

Q16766476_RhetoricalRole.DEFINITION.name: decision tree learning_RhetoricalRole.DEFINITION
Q16766476_RhetoricalRole.DEFINITION.content: Figure I: Decision tree to assist in task identification.

Q1152135_RhetoricalRole.DEFINITION.name: unsupervised learning_RhetoricalRole.DEFINITION
Q1152135_RhetoricalRole.DEFINITION.content: In constrast to that, unsupervised learning refers to tasks where no examples are supplied, and algorithms optimize some general loss function (e.g. genomic species delimitation, see Derkarabetian et al., 2019).

Q334384.name: supervised learning
Q334384.content: machine learning task of learning a function that maps an input to an output based on example input-output pairs

Q334384_RhetoricalRole.DEFINITION.name: supervised learning_RhetoricalRole.DEFINITION
Q334384_RhetoricalRole.DEFINITION.content: In supervised learning, the algorithm is presented with examples for the “correct” execution of the task, and the model is trained to minize the differences its own and the “correct” actions.

concept_593c01bf694a_RhetoricalRole.DEFI.name: Classification task_RhetoricalRole.DEFINITION
concept_593c01bf694a_RhetoricalRole.DEFI.content: if y is discrete (e.g., species classes), it is a classification task,

concept_dc122c3b3285_RhetoricalRole.DEFI.name: Regression task_RhetoricalRole.DEFINITION
concept_dc122c3b3285_RhetoricalRole.DEFI.content: if y is a continuous variable (e.g. biomass), it is a regression task.

Q3414877.name: quest / mission
Q3414877.content: task in video games that a player-controlled character may complete to gain a reward and/or progress the story

Q3414877_RhetoricalRole.DEFINITION.name: quest / mission_RhetoricalRole.DEFINITION
Q3414877_RhetoricalRole.DEFINITION.content: In ML, the different use cases for the algorithms are called tasks.

Q5962346.name: classification scheme
Q5962346.content: system of descriptive information for an arrangement or division of objects into groups based on characteristics, which the objects have in common

Q208042.name: regression analysis
Q208042.content: set of statistical processes for estimating the relationships among variables

Q830687.name: reinforcement learning
Q830687.content: type of machine learning where an agent learns how to behave in an environment by performing actions and receiving rewards or penalties in return, aiming to maximize the cumulative reward over time

Q830687_RhetoricalRole.DEFINITION.name: reinforcement learning_RhetoricalRole.DEFINITION
Q830687_RhetoricalRole.DEFINITION.content: Finally, in reinforcement learning, the Machine Learning algorithm is trained by interacting with a (virtual) environment.

Q830687_RhetoricalRole.STATEMENT.name: reinforcement learning_RhetoricalRole.STATEMENT
Q830687_RhetoricalRole.STATEMENT.content: Reinforcement learning is used in tasks in which the learning depends on executed actions and their produced consequences, for instance, playing strategy computer games such as DOTA (OpenAI et al., 2019) or Starcraft (Vinyals et al., 2019).

concept_61357c174f97_RhetoricalRole.DEFI.name: Training (supervised & reinforcement learning)_RhetoricalRole.DEFINITION
concept_61357c174f97_RhetoricalRole.DEFI.content: In supervised and reinforcement learning, training a model consists of two steps.

Q25048582_RhetoricalRole.DEFINITION.name: Loss functions for classification_RhetoricalRole.DEFINITION
Q25048582_RhetoricalRole.DEFINITION.content: The first step is the definition of a loss function, which measures the current score (performance) of the algorithm in solving a certain task.

Q25048582_RhetoricalRole.STATEMENT.name: Loss functions for classification_RhetoricalRole.STATEMENT
Q25048582_RhetoricalRole.STATEMENT.content: The loss function differs for classification and regression tasks (e.g., mean squared error and categorical cross-entropy are common loss functions for regression and classification tasks).

Q7236587_RhetoricalRole.DEFINITION.name: power optimizer_RhetoricalRole.DEFINITION
Q7236587_RhetoricalRole.DEFINITION.content: The second component is the optimizer, which updates parameters of the algorithm with the goal to increase its performance.

Q7236587_RhetoricalRole.OBJECTIVE.name: power optimizer_RhetoricalRole.OBJECTIVE
Q7236587_RhetoricalRole.OBJECTIVE.content: with the goal to increase its performance.

concept_cb57ee5e4172_RhetoricalRole.DEFI.name: Unsupervised learning (approach)_RhetoricalRole.DEFINITION
concept_cb57ee5e4172_RhetoricalRole.DEFI.content: In unsupervised learning it depends on the method, but a common approach is to use similarities between observations to decide if observations are grouped together or not.

Q2539.name: machine learning
Q2539.content: scientific study of algorithms and statistical models that computer systems use to perform tasks without explicit instructions

Q2539_RhetoricalRole.DEFINITION.name: machine learning_RhetoricalRole.DEFINITION
Q2539_RhetoricalRole.DEFINITION.content: The rising availability of computers around the 1980s allowed not only more refined numerical solutions for classical statistical methods, but also the development of alternative modelling approaches for data analysis and predictions that we collectively refer to as “machine learning”.

Q2539_RhetoricalRole.STATEMENT.name: machine learning_RhetoricalRole.STATEMENT
Q2539_RhetoricalRole.STATEMENT.content: Although these approaches differ in detail, we see their communality in the realization that abandoning the data-generating model (connected to the ability to calculate p-values, CIs and all that) in favor of generic algorithmic structures that can be trained to data often achieves lower errors for predictive tasks (for general Machine Learning principles, see Box 1) (Breiman, 2001b; Shmueli, 2010).

Q192776_RhetoricalRole.STATEMENT.name: artificial neural network_RhetoricalRole.STATEMENT
Q192776_RhetoricalRole.STATEMENT.content: Examples of early Machine Learning algorithms are neural networks (McCulloch & Pitts, 1943), random forest (Breiman, 2001a), and boosted regression trees (Friedman, 2001) (more on these in the section ‘Important ML Algorithms in more detail’).

Q245748.name: random forest

Q245748_RhetoricalRole.STATEMENT.content: Examples of early Machine Learning algorithms are neural networks (McCulloch & Pitts, 1943), random forest (Breiman, 2001a), and boosted regression trees (Friedman, 2001) (more on these in the section ‘Important ML Algorithms in more detail’).

concept_f12564ff610c_RhetoricalRole.STAT.content: The algorithmic nature of the new ML models laxed the necessary distributional assumptions for calculating p-values and CIs and fueled the development of non-parametric approaches

Q893195_RhetoricalRole.DEFINITION.name: Bootstrap_RhetoricalRole.DEFINITION
Q893195_RhetoricalRole.DEFINITION.content: a resampling technique that is often used for estimating CIs on the parameters and predictions of statistical or Machine Learning models.

Q893195_RhetoricalRole.PROBLEM.name: Bootstrap_RhetoricalRole.PROBLEM
Q893195_RhetoricalRole.PROBLEM.content: Since either of these methods require repeated evaluations of the model, their application would be unimageable without computers and can even today be computationally challenging for complex models (more on this in section ‘Why does machine learning work’).

Q5188206_RhetoricalRole.DEFINITION.name: Cross-validation_RhetoricalRole.DEFINITION
Q5188206_RhetoricalRole.DEFINITION.content: cross-validation, where a part of the data is used to train the model and the other part of the data is used to assess the error (Stone, 1974; see Roberts et al., 2017 for cross-validation strategies for structured ecological data).

Q5188206_RhetoricalRole.PROBLEM.name: Cross-validation_RhetoricalRole.PROBLEM

Q113894124_RhetoricalRole.DEFINITION.content: AI refers to algorithms that are capable of achieving similar to human performance in specific decision or recognition tasks.
